pages.x: In 1808 Napoleon forced the king of Spain to give up his throne and put his own brother on it. In the Americas, Spain's colonists had to decide whom to obey. City councils from Caracas to Buenos Aires set up their own governments, at first in the captive king's name, then more and more for themselves.

In New Spain, now Mexico, a village priest, Miguel Hidalgo, rang his church bell in Dolores at dawn on 16 September 1810 and called his people to rise. Tens of thousands of poor farmers and Native people followed him, but his army was beaten, and he was caught and shot in 1811. Mexicans still celebrate his cry on their independence day.

In the south José de San Martín, an Argentine who had fought for Spain against Napoleon, trained an army at Mendoza and in 1817 led it across the Andes by passes nearly 4,000 metres high. He beat the Spanish at Chacabuco and freed Chile with Bernardo O'Higgins, then sailed north and declared Peru independent in 1821.

Simón Bolívar, a rich Venezuelan who had sworn on a hill in Rome to free his homeland, lost battles and was driven into exile more than once. In 1819 he led his army over the freezing Andes, where many died of cold, and surprised the Spanish at Boyacá. The victory freed New Granada, today's Colombia.

Portugal's great colony took a gentler path. Its royal family had fled Napoleon to Rio de Janeiro in 1808. When the king went home, his son Pedro stayed, and in September 1822, by a stream called the Ipiranga, he declared Brazil independent. It became an empire, with Pedro as its first emperor.

Peru was Spain's last stronghold. San Martín met Bolívar at Guayaquil in 1822, then stepped aside and left for Europe; no one knows what they said. In December 1824 Bolívar's general Antonio José de Sucre beat the last big royal army at Ayacucho, high in the Andes. Spanish rule in South America was over.

Bolívar dreamed of one great American nation, but his Gran Colombia, which joined today's Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Panama, fell apart in quarrels. Sick and bitter, he wrote in 1830 that those who had served the revolution had ploughed the sea. He died that December, aged 47.

In under twenty years Spain lost an empire it had held for three centuries, and new countries were born from Mexico to Argentina. But independence often left the old landowners in charge, and many of the new states fell into civil wars and rule by strongmen. Bolívar is honoured across the continent; Bolivia is named after him.
pts: San Martín crossed the Andes in 1817
Brazil broke away from Portugal in 1822
Ayacucho ended Spanish rule in South America, 1824
